title: ‘A blanket order would go too far’: Madras high court refuses to restrict protests against court rulings

ai.summary: The Madras High Court refused to ban protests against court rulings, stating citizens have a right to disagree with judgments but must avoid targeting judges personally. Authorities must assess protest permits on a case-by-case basis under the BNSS law.

facts.claim: The Madras high court refused to restrict public protests against court rulings
facts.quote: The court said authorities must assess applications seeking permission for meetings, marches or protests relating to judicial matters on a "case-by-case basis."

facts.claim: Citizens have an undeniable right to disagree with a judgment
facts.quote: The Madras high court has refused to restrict public protests against court rulings and emphasised that citizens have an undeniable right to disagree with a judgment, underscoring citizens' right to "question and peacefully protest" against judicial decisions.

facts.claim: Authorities must assess applications seeking permission for meetings, marches or protests relating to judicial matters on a "case-by-case basis"
facts.quote: In an order passed on Friday, October 30, a bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G Arul Murugan said authorities must assess applications seeking permission for meetings, marches or protests relating to judicial matters on a "case-by-case basis," using their powers under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and local police laws.

facts.claim: A blanket order completely banning all public discussions or peaceful gatherings concerning court rulings would go too far
facts.quote: "A blanket order completely banning all public discussions or peaceful gatherings concerning court rulings would go too far. It would infringe upon legitimate democratic expression," the high court said.

facts.claim: The court directed the state and police authorities in Tamil Nadu to "deny" permission to any gathering aimed at "personally targeting a sitting judge."
facts.quote: However, the court directed the state and police authorities in Tamil Nadu to "deny" permission to any gathering aimed at "personally targeting a sitting judge."

ai.background_note: The Madras High Court clarified the legal boundaries between criticizing judicial decisions and attacking individual judges, emphasizing case-by-case assessment of protest permits under BNSS law.
